title: Exterior Lighting: What Each System Does
introduction:
The Mustang’s exterior lighting is a small stage crew: some lamps light the road, some announce your intentions, and several share the same housing. I start by matching each lighting job to its lamps, switches and control modules. That makes the repeated component names useful rather than alphabet soup.

Read the equipment and market qualifiers closely, especially the China-only features and the alternative mirror or hood turn signals. This overview explains the components and normal behavior described here; electrical testing, adjustment and replacement require their matching procedures.

edits.text: The headlamp system brings together the following lamp hardware, driver controls and electronic modules:
edits.why: I read this as a system map: the visible lamps are only part of the arrangement.
LH means left-hand; this identifies the multifunction switch on the left side of the steering column.
This controller coordinates many body electrical functions and exchanges information with other modules.
This is the electronic interface for switches on and around the steering wheel.

edits.text: The High Intensity Discharge (HID) headlamps provide a dual-beam pattern, with a replaceable High Intensity Discharge (HID) bulb in each headlamp assembly. Except in China, the LED signature lamps are also integrated into the headlamp assemblies.
edits.why: The signature lighting shares the headlamp housing. LED means light emitting diode; HID identifies the headlamp bulb technology.

edits.text: China-only headlamps include manual headlamp leveling.
edits.why: Keep this market distinction in mind when identifying the equipment fitted to the car.

edits.text: The DRL, or daytime running lamps, system uses these components:
Where fitted, the DRL system operates the fog lamp assemblies as the daytime running lamps.
edits.why: Here the fog lamp hardware does double duty. Seeing these lamps illuminated does not, by itself, tell you which lighting function is using them.

edits.text: The autolamp system combines these components:

Autolamps switch the exterior lamps on and off automatically in response to light conditions. After the ignition is turned OFF, they keep the exterior lamps on for a selected delay; the factory default is 20 seconds. Use the message center controls to adjust that delay up to approximately 3 minutes.
edits.why: The delayed switch-off gives the lighting a brief curtain call after shutdown. I check the selected delay before treating lamps that remain on briefly as unexpected behavior.

edits.text: The stoplamp system includes the brake input, lamps and modules below:
Body Control Module B (BCMB), except China
The stoplamp switch is on the brake pedal assembly. Applying the brake pedal supplies voltage to the rear lamps and the high mounted stoplamp.
edits.why: The pedal supplies the braking input, while the rear lamps and high mounted stoplamp provide the visible braking signal.

edits.text: The turn signal system includes the following lamps, switches and modules. Match the equipment qualifiers to the car:
edits.why: The mirror and hood entries describe alternative turn signal arrangements.

edits.text: Front turn lamps, integrated into the front marker lamp assemblies
Exterior mirror assemblies, on cars without hood turn signals
Hood turn signal lamps, on cars without exterior mirror turn signals
Hazard flasher lamp switch, integrated into the FCIM
edits.why: The hazard switch is part of the named control assembly.

edits.text: Body Control Module B (BCMB), except China
DDM — driver door module, if equipped with memory seat
PDM — passenger door module, if equipped with memory seat
Moving the LH steering column multifunction switch to LH TURN or RH TURN makes the turn lamps on the corresponding side flash on and off.
edits.why: The selected position identifies which side should signal: LH is left-hand and RH is right-hand.

edits.text: With the hazard function active, all the turn lamps flash on and off.
edits.why: Hazards use the turn lamps together, giving the same lamp hardware a different signaling job.

edits.text: Parking, Rear and License Plate Lamps
The parking, rear and license plate lighting system includes these lamps, controls and modules:
Body Control Module B (BCMB), except China
The front marker lamp assemblies contain both the front parking lamps and the front side marker lamps.
edits.why: I use the assembly name to locate the shared housing, then distinguish the lighting functions within it.

edits.text: The rear parking lamps are built into the rear lamp assemblies.
edits.why: The rear assembly appears in several system lists because its housing serves several lighting jobs.

edits.text: The front fog lamp system uses these components:
Front fog lamp switch, integrated into the headlamp switch
The front fog lamps can be switched on when all these conditions are met: the ignition is in RUN, the parking lamps are on, and the high beams are off.
edits.why: I check the whole combination before judging fog lamp behavior. Each condition belongs to the normal operating requirements.

edits.text: The China-only rear fog lamp system includes these components:
Rear fog lamp switch, integrated into the headlamp switch
The rear fog lamp can be switched on when the ignition is in RUN and the headlamps are on.
edits.why: This function requires the headlamps to be on; keep its operating conditions distinct from those of the front fog lamps.

edits.text: The reversing lamp system includes these components, with the transmission type determining which switch or sensor applies:
Reversing lamp switch, for manual transmission
Transmission range sensor, for automatic transmission
Selecting REVERSE illuminates the reversing lamps. They are located at the bottom of the rear bumper fascia.
edits.why: I use the bumper location to distinguish the reversing lights from the other lighting functions housed in the rear lamp assemblies.
